title: Al-Hakam, the Judge
hook: the Judge, whose judgment is final
tomorrow: fair, even against your own family? one verse says yes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Basir: a warning to one man, company for Moses and Aaron. The line: seen. Today, what the one who sees does with what He sees.

A stranger posts one blurry paragraph about a fight with her sister, asking: was I wrong? Underneath, hundreds of verdicts from people who will never meet either of them. Handing out verdicts feels good. It feels a little like power. A man in Arabia had that power for real. His people brought him their disputes, and both sides left content, so they gave him a proud nickname: Abu al-Hakam, father of the judge. Yesterday's question was why the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, changed it. Here's what happened when they met.
screen: `HUNDREDS OF VERDICTS.` → `A MAN THEY CALLED THE JUDGE.` → `THEN HE MEETS THE PROPHET.`

segments.voice: The Prophet heard the nickname and said: Allah is al-Hakam, and judgment belongs to Him, so why are you called that? The man explained. When my people disagree, I judge between them, and both sides are satisfied. And the Prophet said: how good this is. Notice that. The peacemaking wasn't the problem. It was praised. Then he asked about the man's children, heard that the eldest was Shurayh, and said: then you are Abu Shurayh. A father's name, after his son. The work stayed. The title went back to its owner. That's today's Name. Al-Hakam, the Judge. People still settle disputes, run courts, call a foul a foul. But the last word on a person, on what's inside them and where they end up, isn't ours to hold. The Qur'an asks it as a question, in Surah at-Tin: "Is not Allah the most conclusive of all judges?" Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: in this hadith, a man who settled fights well got a new name, after his kid. One verdict to set down, today, could be the one about someone you barely know.
screen: `ALLAH IS AL-HAKAM.` · `HOW GOOD THIS IS.` · `THEN YOU ARE ABU SHURAYH.` · `THE MOST CONCLUSIVE OF JUDGES.` · then, large: `HE JUDGES.`

segments.voice: Pick up something small in each hand: a pen, a coin, a key. Feel the two weights. Let one of them stand for a verdict you've been carrying about someone this week. Set that one down on the table, let go of it, and leave it there for the sit.
screen: `ONE WEIGHT IN EACH HAND.` · `SET ONE VERDICT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Al-Hakam. The Judge, whose judgment is final, and whose title a good peacemaker gave back.
Hold on to this: he judges, so the last word on a person is never yours to carry. Go gently.

howItsDone: Muslims settle disputes through judges, arbiters and family elders, while holding that final judgment of a person belongs to Allah; Surah at-Tin closes by asking whether Allah is not the most conclusive of judges.

fork.setup: you saw a teammate copy answers on a quiz. your friends want your verdict: is she just a bad person? what fits Al-Hakam?
options: tell the teacher if it matters, and leave the verdict on her as a person to God.
say yes, she's a cheater; facts are facts and people should know.

fork.reveal: a foul can be called a foul; the man who judged disputes was praised. what goes back to Allah is the last word on who she is.

original.note: Arabic: the Judge, the one whose ruling is final. the title the Prophet said belongs to Allah.

trapdoor: what you thought: God as a strict courtroom judge.
what it means: the one whose judgment is final, so people can settle matters fairly without claiming the last word on anyone.
what a scholar hears: the hadith of Abu Shurayh (Sunan Abi Dawud 4955; Sunan an-Nasa'i 5387), cited in discussions of names and titles reserved for Allah; 95:8 as a closing question.
guess: the Judge, whose ruling is the final one
the one who forbids every human court
the one who judges only on the last day
